excerpt: How long workers' compensation benefits last in Georgia and South Carolina, and what determines when they stop.
keyTakeaways: Workers' comp benefit duration varies by state and disability type: Georgia caps TTD at 400 weeks from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261), with no cap for catastrophic injuries while the disability lasts; South Carolina allows 500 weeks (S.C. Code § 42-9-10), or life for paraplegia, quadriplegia or physical brain damage (S.C. Code § 42-9-10(C)). Medical benefits outlast wage benefits but are not unlimited: Georgia covers up to 400 weeks from injury unless the injury is catastrophic (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200), and South Carolina covers treatment the Commission finds will lessen your disability (S.C. Code § 42-15-60). To maximize benefits, follow your treatment plan, challenge premature MMI declarations, and never accept a settlement without legal review. When benefits end, options include SSDI, third-party lawsuits, and vocational rehabilitation.

faqs.question: What is the maximum time you can receive workers' compensation in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia caps temporary total disability (TTD) at 400 weeks (~7.7 years) under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261. Temporary partial disability (TPD) is capped at 350 weeks. However, catastrophic injuries — spinal cord injuries with severe paralysis, amputations with loss of use, severe brain injuries, severe burns, total blindness, or any injury that keeps you from doing your old job or any other work available in substantial numbers — are not subject to the 400-week cap and can be paid for life (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-200.1, 34-9-261). Medical benefits last up to 400 weeks from the injury for injuries since July 1, 2013, or for life if the injury is catastrophic (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200).

faqs.question: What is the maximum time you can receive workers' compensation in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina caps TTD at 500 weeks (~9.6 years) under S.C. Code § 42-9-10, and TPD at 340 weeks. Totally and permanently disabled workers left paraplegic, quadriplegic or with physical brain damage receive benefits for life (S.C. Code § 42-9-10(C)). Medical benefits continue as long as the Commission finds treatment will lessen your disability, but can end after a year without authorized treatment or after a settlement (S.C. Code § 42-15-60; S.C. Code Regs. 67-801(E)).

faqs.question: Can I receive workers' comp and Social Security disability at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, but there is an offset. Federal law limits your combined workers' comp and SSDI benefits to 80% of your average current earnings (generally your highest recent earnings before the disability) until you reach full retirement age (42 U.S.C. § 424a). If the combined amount exceeds that threshold, your SSDI payment is reduced. An initial SSDI decision generally takes 6 to 8 months, so apply early. An attorney can help structure a workers' comp settlement to minimize the SSDI reduction.

faqs.question: What happens when my workers' comp benefits run out?
faqs.answer: When wage replacement benefits end, your options include: medical benefits (which can continue after wage benefits end — for up to 400 weeks in most Georgia cases), Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a personal injury lawsuit if a third party caused your injury, and vocational rehabilitation to retrain for new employment (through workers' comp in Georgia only for catastrophic injuries; otherwise through state vocational rehabilitation agencies).

faqs.question: Should I accept a lump-sum workers' comp settlement?
faqs.answer: A lump-sum settlement provides guaranteed money but closes out your claim — you generally cannot reopen it for additional benefits later. Never accept a settlement without attorney review. An experienced lawyer can evaluate whether the offer accounts for your future medical needs, remaining disability benefits, and permanent impairment.

faqs.question: How can I prevent the insurer from cutting my benefits short?
faqs.answer: Follow your treatment plan consistently, do not return to work prematurely, get an independent medical opinion if you disagree with the insurer's doctor, challenge premature benefit terminations through a hearing, and hire an attorney early. Insurers use tactics like premature MMI declarations, low impairment ratings, and surveillance to justify ending benefits — legal representation helps counter these strategies.

metaDescription: Georgia pays TTD up to 400 weeks, South Carolina up to 500. How catastrophic injuries, medical limits and settlements shape how long workers' comp lasts.
